blocks.text: 1. LoRA
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446293541-800839899.png

Full Fine-Tuning's own closing recap, already covered in Full Fine-Tuning, pointed forward here. LoRA, a technique addressing the storage and compute cost of full fine-tuning, is one of the most widely used efficient fine-tuning methods.
It genuinely trains a small pair of added matrices instead of touching the original weights at all, a mechanism explored in full throughout this topic.
2. Recapping The Preview

This connects back to Full Fine-Tuning's own closing recap, already covered in Full Fine-Tuning. LoRA was genuinely previewed there as addressing the storage and compute cost of full fine-tuning, briefly described in that earlier topic.
This topic genuinely gives it the complete, dedicated treatment already promised, exploring every detail already hinted at generally in that earlier topic.
3. Freezing The Original Weights
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446293541-268648661.png
This connects back to updating every single weight, already covered in Full Fine-Tuning. LoRA genuinely keeps every single original pretrained weight completely frozen.
Genuinely none of the original, already-pretrained weights ever get directly modified at all, a genuinely fundamental departure from full fine-tuning explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 4. Adding A Small Trainable Matrix Pair

blocks.alt: Adding A Small Trainable Matrix Pair
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446293541-65682046.png
This connects back to freezing the original weights, already covered in this topic. Alongside each genuinely frozen weight matrix, LoRA genuinely adds a small pair of new, trainable matrices.
Only that genuinely small, added pair actually gets trained; the original matrix genuinely stays untouched, the exact core mechanism explored throughout the rest of this topic.
5. Low Rank Decomposition
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446293541-978867731.png

This connects back to adding a small trainable matrix pair, already covered in this topic. Those two genuinely small matrices are deliberately genuinely low rank, far smaller than the original weight matrix.
Genuinely multiplying them back together approximates a genuinely full-sized update using far fewer parameters, the genuinely core mathematical trick explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 6. Dramatically Fewer Trainable Parameters
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446293541-110660310.png
This connects back to low rank decomposition, already covered in this topic. This genuinely low rank structure genuinely reduces trainable parameters by orders of magnitude.

This directly solves the compute and memory cost already covered as full fine-tuning's own limitation in Full Fine-Tuning, a genuinely direct, practical payoff explored throughout the rest of this topic.
7. Swappable Lightweight Adapters
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446293541-438307117.png

This connects back to dramatically fewer trainable parameters, already covered in this topic. Because the genuinely original model stays frozen, each task genuinely only needs its own small pair of matrices saved.
Genuinely swapping between tasks means genuinely swapping only that small, lightweight adapter, not the entire model, directly solving the storage multiplication already covered in Full Fine-Tuning.

blocks.text: 8. Merging LoRA Weights At Inference Time

This connects back to swappable lightweight adapters, already covered in this topic. At genuinely inference time, the small LoRA matrices can genuinely get merged directly back into the original weights.
This produces a genuinely single combined model with genuinely no extra runtime cost compared to the original, a genuinely elegant final step explored throughout the rest of this topic.

10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a simplified low rank matrix pair, already covered in this topic, approximating an update to a frozen weight.

code.content:
def matmul(a, b):
    # already covered as multiplying low rank matrices back together in this topic
    rows_a, cols_a = len(a), len(a[0])
    cols_b = len(b[0])
    result = [[0.0] * cols_b for _ in range(rows_a)]
    for i in range(rows_a):
        for j in range(cols_b):
            result[i][j] = sum(a[i][k] * b[k][j] for k in range(cols_a))
    return result

# already covered as freezing the original weights in this topic
frozen_weight = [[0.9, 0.1], [0.2, 0.8]]

# already covered as a small, low rank trainable matrix pair in this topic
matrix_a = [[0.1], [0.05]]        # shape 2x1, genuinely low rank
matrix_b = [[0.3, -0.2]]          # shape 1x2, genuinely low rank

lora_update = matmul(matrix_a, matrix_b)  # already covered as low rank decomposition in this topic
print(f"LoRA update, from a genuinely small matrix pair (already covered in this topic): {lora_update}")

# already covered as merging LoRA weights at inference time in this topic
merged_weight = [[frozen_weight[i][j] + lora_update[i][j] for j in range(2)] for i in range(2)]
print(f"Frozen original weight (already covered in this topic): {frozen_weight}")
print(f"Merged weight at inference time: {merged_weight}")

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: LoRA trains a small pair of added matrices instead of touching the original pretrained weights.
Every original weight stays completely frozen; none of it ever gets directly modified.
A small pair of new, trainable matrices gets added alongside each frozen weight matrix.
These matrices are deliberately low rank, approximating a full update with far fewer parameters.
This low rank structure reduces trainable parameters by orders of magnitude compared to full fine-tuning.
Because the base model stays frozen, each task only needs its own small adapter matrices saved.
Swapping between tasks means swapping only that lightweight adapter, not the entire model.
At inference time, LoRA matrices can merge back into the original weights with no extra runtime cost.
